documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) applications are transforming the traditional language learning paradigm by leveraging AI technologies to provide a more efficient, convenient, and personalized learning experience. Despite the integration of AI technologies into MALL applications, prior studies have overlooked the critical role of AI service quality in shaping learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance within these applications. This study addresses this research gap by leveraging social support theory to develop a research model that examines how the AI service quality of AI-powered MALL applications influences social support, specifically informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support are further analyzed to determine their effects on learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance. A total of 978 valid samples were collected from users of AI-powered MALL applications and analyzed using the partial least-squares method. The results indicate that AI service quality significantly enhances users’ perceptions of informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support positively influence learning satisfaction and learning performance. Furthermore, the mediation analysis revealed that informational, emotional, and appraisal support act as partial mediators in the relationships between AI service quality and learning satisfaction and between AI service quality and learning performance. This study contributes to the literature by revealing how AI service quality, social support, and learning satisfaction and performance interact in the context of AI-enabled MALL applications. We also offer practical insights for improving the user experience and maximizing the learning outcomes of AI-driven MALL applications.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) has become a large influence on students and teachers in the mathematics classroom. Specifically, researchers found that genAI tools could solve probability questions such as “What is the probability of drawing the Queen of Hearts from a standard deck of playing cards on the first try?” These researchers also stated that the genAI tools could not be trusted when solving, “Three cards are lying face down in front of me. Two are face cards, and there are no spades. No card is next to a card of the same color. What are the odds that the card on the left is the Queen of Hearts?” However, it is unclear whether that statement is true. Thus, we verified these findings by investigating four genAI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Co-Pilot, and Claude AI) on their ability to complete the identified probability task to determine when genAI can be trusted to perform probability calculation. Using the results of this investigation, we examined these genAI models using their responses and the predictions made by the genAI trainer. The investigation implies that developing mathematical validity requires intentional instruction, including teaching students how to compare genAI’s explanations, conducting GenAI Triangulation Process, cross-checking results using independent methods or alternative tools, and justifying whether an answer is mathematically sound.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This article aims to analyze the relevance of cognitive development and comprehensive ethical education in the critical and responsible use of generative artificial intelligence, with the purpose of preventing and counteracting the potential dehumanizing consequences that could affect the human condition in the twenty-first century. From a theoretical-analytical approach, it argues for the need for early digital education that fosters intellectual development and prevents technology from becoming a source of dependency. It highlights that education constitutes a key tool to counter cognitive laziness and the improper use of intelligent systems by university students, to the detriment of their critical reasoning capacities. It concludes that understanding the relevance of brain development and its relationship with cognitive learning processes constitutes an essential foundation for the formation of critical thinking and for the adoption of a responsible ethical approach to the use of artificial intelligence. Integrating these three components –cognitive development, critical thinking, and technological ethics—is indispensable for guiding the application of generative artificial intelligence toward pedagogical and humanistic ends that strengthen cognitive competencies, autonomy, and the reflective capacity of human beings in the twenty-first century.

documents.abstract: This chapter establishes the ethical, legal, and societal foundations of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science, conceptualizing AI as a socio-technical system whose legitimacy depends on fairness, transparency, accountability, and respect for athlete autonomy. It critically examines the implications of algorithmic bias, data imbalance, and limited generalizability, demonstrating how AI systems may unintentionally reinforce structural inequalities across gender, age, and performance levels. The chapter further addresses the “black box” problem and emphasizes the importance of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods in enhancing transparency and trust in high-stakes decision-making contexts such as injury prediction, talent identification, and performance evaluation. Particular attention is given to power asymmetries between athletes and institutions, highlighting risks related to data ownership, surveillance, and the erosion of informed consent. From a regulatory perspective, the chapter analyses key frameworks including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, with a focus on high-risk AI systems in sport. Through applied case studies, it demonstrates how ethical principles, human oversight, and governance mechanisms can be operationalized in practice. The chapter contributes to the development of responsible AI in Sports Science by integrating ethical theory, legal standards, and applied methodological considerations.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce chemistry lesson plans containing objectives, activities, resources, and assessments, but evaluating their educational contribution requires different kinds of evidence. This critical narrative review examines GenAI-assisted planning for secondary chemistry through three objects of evaluation: the written plan, teachers' professional reasoning and revisions, and students' learning. Seven recent chemistry and science education studies provide the principal contemporary evidence, interpreted alongside research on pedagogical content knowledge, chemical representations, and constructive alignment. The synthesis identifies useful planning support while showing why completed templates, teacher perceptions, and classroom outcomes require separate interpretation. Chemistry-specific review should examine the conditions attached to scientific claims, the connections among representations, the reasoning elicited by tasks, and the responses that trigger instructional adjustment. A worked illustration using electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate demonstrates how these criteria translate into changes to objectives, diagnostic questions, and follow-up teaching decisions. The article proposes a planning-review procedure and a teacher-education assignment that make justified revisions visible through planning records and discussion. Future studies can connect these records with classroom enactment and student explanations while separating AI assistance from additional opportunities to revise. The review positions teachers' transformation of generated materials as the link between the availability of planning support and the quality of the learning opportunities eventually offered to students.

AI (Artificial Intelligence) has significantly influenced and transformed the way teaching, learning and assessment occur. In this era, AI has become the center of discussion and debate among educators and students in programming education. As such, current evaluation systems seek to provide immediate feedback by leveraging AI capabilities. Feedback is important because it gives both the student and the teacher a holistic view of the learning progress. However, there remains a lack of adequate solutions for evaluating and linking prior knowledge to current knowledge (learning transition) in programming education. To close the gap, we developed an AI model (based on the Google Gemini Application Programming Interface (API) and also following Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM)) that evaluates and categorises program code into SOLO (Structure of Observed Learning Outcome)-adapted stages. The aim of the AI model is to evaluate two program codes by comparing the earlier version with the current code to provide informed feedback. High-level categories of learning transitions include progression (improvement), regression (learning has deteriorated), and no learning (stagnation). The model was tested in all 25 possibilities (learning transitions) to assess its capacity on the given synthetic test cases.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced new possibilities for machine translation (MT) by allowing translation outputs to be shaped through natural-language instructions. However, evidence about how different prompt configurations affect translation quality relative to established neural machine translation (NMT) systems remains limited, particularly for Indonesian–English translation. This exploratory mixed-methods comparative study examines three prompt configurations applied to ChatGPT and compares the resulting outputs with DeepL and Google Translate across six tourism, promotional, and proverbial texts. Translation outputs were assessed computationally using cross-lingual cosine similarity from text-embedding-3-large as an exploratory indicator of semantic proximity and qualitatively through evaluations by three professional translators focusing on accuracy, appropriateness, naturalness, and discourse style. In the observed sample, DeepL and the baseline-prompt condition tended to obtain higher similarity scores for factual tourism texts, whereas contextual- and persona-prompt outputs received comparatively favorable expert evaluations in selected promotional and culturally embedded cases. Contextual prompting also produced additions beyond the wording shown in the source excerpts, indicating a trade-off between rhetorical adaptation and source fidelity. Because the corpus is small, the prompt conditions bundle several instructional features, repeated generations were not documented, and some reproducibility metadata were not archived, the findings are interpreted descriptively rather than as causal or statistically generalizable effects. The study therefore highlights a genre- and criterion-sensitive relationship among prompt configuration, semantic preservation, and functional translation quality, while underscoring the need for human verification of adaptive LLM translations.

This study presents a comparative evaluation of traditional machine learning algorithms and state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) in classification tasks using structured data. The analysis is conducted on the widely used Iris dataset, which consists of measurements from three different flower species and serves as a benchmark in machine learning literature. The performance of classical algorithms, including logistic regression, K-nearest neighbors, decision trees, and random forest, is examined based on well-established evaluation metrics. Following the implementation of these algorithms in Python (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE, USA), their results are compared with the numerical reasoning capabilities of LLMs, including GPT-5.3 Instant (OpenAI, San Francisco, California, USA), Gemini 3.0 Flash (Google LLC, Mountain View, California, USA), Copilot (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, USA), and Qwen 3.5 (Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China). The LLMbased evaluations are performed by providing algorithm-specific prompts and analyzing the generated outputs. The findings indicate that, beyond their natural language processing capabilities, LLMs can achieve competitive performance in structured data classification tasks, reaching accuracy levels between 90% and 97%. Among the evaluated models, Gemini 3.0 Flash demonstrates superior performance by more effectively capturing multivariate relationships within the dataset. Overall, the results suggest that transformer-based architectures can serve as strong alternatives to traditional deterministic algorithms in numerical classification problems, highlighting the evolving role of LLMs as general-purpose data analysis tools.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet potential risks accompany over-reliance on these tools. Grounded in Rogers’ diffusion-of-innovations theory, the present study employed a mixed-methods design. Four waves of independent cross-sectional quantitative data (T1–T4, N = 788) were complemented by semi-structured interviews with 20 undergraduate students. Key patterns emerged as follows: (i) Across later waves, the direct association between external regulation and intrinsic motivation attenuated, while the indirect association operating via identified regulation strengthened. The path from identified regulation to intrinsic motivation was the only relationship that demonstrated significant cross-pair differences while satisfying invariance requirements for all three wave-pair comparisons. Because scalar invariance could not be established, this pattern is interpreted solely as a descriptive group-level temporal trend and should not be read as evidence of intra-individual change. (ii) AI-assisted creativity showed the largest and most consistent downward shift: estimates in later waves were significantly lower relative to the T1 baseline, with effect sizes increasing progressively (Δ = −0.391 to −0.549; d = −0.61 to −0.95; all p < 0.001 following Holm correction). This pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting for gender, year of study, and academic major, and held up in four predefined subsamples as well as under propensity-score weighting. (iii) The linkage between AI dependency and creativity was significantly positive only at T3 and became negative but non-significant at T4, pointing to a conditional, wave-specific association rather than a stable linear relationship. (iv) Observed wave-level differences for AI dependency and intrinsic motivation did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. Sensitivity tests yielded only two significant coefficients for AI dependency and none for intrinsic motivation; accordingly, these fluctuations are not given substantive theoretical interpretation. Retrospective qualitative accounts provided supplementary process-oriented context: participants reported initial exposure to AI driven by prevailing social trends, sustained use based on perceived utility, subsequent disappointment in unreliable or misleading outputs, and eventual shifts toward more strategic, self-regulated engagement. Given their retrospective nature, interview narratives were not used to triangulate or validate the quantitative findings. Collectively, this work suggests that as AI-supported learning becomes normalized within a diffusion-driven context, group-level indicators of students’ subjective creative experiences tend to decline. Higher-education institutions may therefore prioritize protecting learners’ creative agency as an explicit educational goal.

Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Industrial maintenance generates near miss narratives that may reveal weaknesses in energy isolation, equipment integrity, permit coordination and other safety barriers. However, interpreting these reports requires contextual judgement, and an automated summary can conceal missing evidence or produce unjustified conclusions. This conceptual paper proposes an evidence-linked artificial intelligence framework for identifying reported barrier degradation and supporting accountable human review. The framework combines a controlled barrier taxonomy, source-linked extraction, retrieval from approved site documents, uncertainty handling and verification of corrective actions. Its central research proposition is that the value of AI should be evaluated through the quality of barrier decisions and the completeness of supporting evidence, rather than classification accuracy alone. A staged mixed methods protocol is specified, including expert annotation, temporal and site-separated testing, comparison with simpler methods, a randomised reviewer study and a prospective shadow deployment. Primary outcomes concern detection of expert-adjudicated barrier concerns, unsupported assertions and reviewer decision quality. Incident reduction is reserved for later investigation and is not inferred from report processing performance. No field dataset, implemented prototype or empirical results are presented. The contribution is a testable research design that connects explainable AI with practical safety assurance while retaining operational authority with competent personnel

This chapter examines the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Sports Science, addressing the growing need for transparency, interpretability, and trust in data-driven decision-making. As machine learning and deep learning models become increasingly complex, their opacity presents significant challenges for practitioners working in performance analysis, injury prevention, and athlete management. The chapter conceptualizes interpretability as a continuum and introduces XAI as a methodological framework that complements predictive accuracy with human-understandable explanations. The chapter systematically presents key approaches to explainability, distinguishing between inherently interpretable models and post hoc explanation techniques such as SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients. It further discusses emerging paradigms, including neuro-symbolic Artificial Intelligence, which aim to integrate data-driven learning with structured domain knowledge. Beyond methodological considerations, the chapter highlights the practical value of XAI in enhancing trust, supporting decision-making, enabling model debugging, ensuring compliance with ethical standards, and facilitating knowledge discovery. Through applied case studies in football and basketball, the chapter demonstrates how XAI methods can be operationalized in real-world sport contexts to improve injury-risk monitoring and tactical analysis. Overall, XAI is positioned as a foundational component of Responsible Artificial Intelligence, enabling more transparent, interpretable, and ethically grounded applications in sports analytics and performance modelling.

Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are in-creasingly being considered for critical applications such as healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and autonomous transporta-tion. These systems consist of multiple intelligent agents that can independently perceive information, reason about their environment, communicate with other agents, and execute deci-sions. Although multi-agent architectures provide flexibility and scalability, their distributed decision-making process can make the overall system difficult to understand, audit, and verify. Existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) primarily fo-cus on explaining individual machine-learning predictions. They provide limited support for representing collaborative reasoning, inter-agent communication, conflicts, and collective decisions. This paper proposes an Explainable Decision Graph (EDG) framework for representing the reasoning process of autonomous multi-agent systems in a structured and interpretable form. The proposed framework models agents, observations, evi-dence, communications, intermediate decisions, conflicts, verifi-cation events, and final actions as interconnected graph com-ponents. A verification layer enables decision pathways to be examined against predefined safety and policy constraints. The resulting graph can provide different levels of explanations for end users, developers, and auditors. The paper defines an experimental methodology using multi-agent execution traces and proposes evaluation through ex-planation fidelity, completeness, decision traceability, human comprehensibility, decision accuracy, explanation consistency, and computational overhead. Empirical numerical results are intentionally reserved for the implementation and evaluation stage.

Conflict resolution is essential for teachers. Pre-service teachers (PSTs) often struggle to connect coursework with classroom practice, especially in multi-role conflicts. Artificial intelligence (AI) simulations may offer a low-risk environment. This study examined PSTs’ conflict-resolution practices in an AI-based multi-agent setting where virtual participants were available within the same conflict scenario. We developed a chatbot through which 20 PSTs interacted with an aggressor, an accomplice, a victim, parents, and a tutor in a peer-conflict scenario. Using dialogue logs, we applied inductive qualitative content analysis and lag sequential analysis to examine behavioural transitions. The analysis identified two complementary findings. First, PSTs’ strategies varied by student-agent role. When addressing aggressors, they tended to use guiding reflection, emotional support, surface threat, and role endowment; when addressing accomplices, they more often used positive encouragement, guiding reflection, home-school collaboration, and emotional support; and when addressing victims, they relied on home-school collaboration, positive relationship guidance, and emotional support. Second, PSTs’ engagement with AI guidance followed four pathways: relying on AI-generated suggestions, iterative inquiry with AI, doubting AI-generated suggestions, and bypassing AI-generated suggestions. These findings suggest that PSTs selectively negotiated role-specific cues and AI guidance, making visible situated professional judgement in AI-supported conflict-resolution practice.
topics: Education for Peace and Conflict Resolution

documents.abstract: Legal AI research often evaluates large language models (LLMs) on legal reasoning tasks under the assumption that relevant facts are already structured and available. This assumption overlooks a prior and practically consequential stage of legal work: fact construction, namely the transformation of incomplete, fragmented, and interactionally disclosed information into coherent factual narratives. This study conceptualizes fact construction as a distinct evaluation layer in legal AI and introduces a practice-grounded framework for assessing it in AI-assisted legal consultation. Rather than proposing a legal advice system or doctrinal rule-matching architecture, we use a role-separated multi-agent workflow consisting of a fact-constrained Litigant Twin, a structured-questioning LegalAider, a NarrativeAgent for factual synthesis, and an Evaluator for factual-alignment assessment. Using 100 de-identified legal clinic consultation records, we evaluate multiple LLMs under rubric-based assessment, comparing generated factual narratives against original human-authored consultation records in terms of factual accuracy, completeness, and consistency. The results show that LLM-based agents can generate usable factual narratives under constrained conditions, particularly when cases are internally consistent, limited to a single dispute, and supported by clear actor-role relationships. However, cross-model evaluator agreement remains moderate, and outlier analysis reveals recurring structural sources of failure, including anonymization-induced referential ambiguity, third-party reporting, multi-episode case complexity, and numerically dense facts. These findings suggest that reliability in AI-assisted legal consultation depends not only on model capability, but also on interaction design, data representation, institutional record-keeping, and human oversight. By treating fact construction as a distinct analytical layer, this article contributes a practice-grounded framework for evaluating responsible LLM integration in legal settings and highlights the need for factual grounding, contestability, and human-supervised review before downstream legal analysis begins.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of financial self-efficacy in the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and the perceived effectiveness of detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks. The study addresses a behavioral and institutional gap in the literature by explaining how AI-supported monitoring capabilities may be translated into effective regulatory action through employees’ confidence in interpreting and using AI-generated outputs. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected from 115 employees working in compliance, Shariah compliance, Shariah supervision, internal audit, auditing, and risk management functions in Jordanian Islamic banks. The questionnaire consisted of 35 items measuring AI adoption, financial self-efficacy, perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness, and demographic characteristics. The data were analyzed using reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, standardized multiple regression, and regression-based mediation analysis. The results indicate that AI adoption has a statistically significant positive direct effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness after accounting for financial self-efficacy (β = 0.296, p = 0.001). AI adoption also has a significant positive effect on financial self-efficacy ( β = 0.640, p < 0.001), while financial self-efficacy has a significant positive effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness ( β = 0.491, p < 0.001). The mediation analysis shows a significant indirect effect of AI adoption on perceived detection effectiveness through financial self-efficacy (indirect effect = 0.314, Sobel z = 4.806, p < 0.001). The VAF value of 51.46% indicates complementary partial mediation. The findings suggest that AI adoption contributes to perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness not only through technological capabilities but also through employees’ financial self-efficacy. The study recommends integrating AI-supported monitoring systems with structured training, human-in-the-loop governance, and Shariah-sensitive regulatory procedures in Islamic banks.

This chapter examines artificial intelligence (AI) as a force that reorganizes firms, platforms, and market structure. AI affects competition not only by lowering costs, but also by changing the industrial assets that matter: proprietary data, compute infrastructure, model capability, specialized talent, distribution channels, and the ability to run continuous experiments. The chapter explains why AI can reinforce superstar firm dynamics, how data can generate increasing returns without being a simple monopoly input, and why platform markets require a two-sided rather than purely product market view. It also studies algorithmic pricing and the possibility that learning systems may facilitate collusive outcomes even without explicit human agreement. The central message is deliberately balanced: AI may intensify concentration when feedback loops between users, data, models, and capital are strong, but it can also lower entry barriers when general-purpose models, cloud infrastructure, and open-source tools become broadly accessible. The policy problem is therefore not to punish scale as such, but to distinguish productive scale from exclusionary control over the bottlenecks of the AI economy.

documents.abstract: Abstract There remains much more to Artificial Intelligence than understanding how to learn with neural networks. Inspired in part by how babies, and humans in general, tend to choose for themselves what (and when ) to learn in addition to how to learn, this article discusses similar opportunities, in the areas of multiagent systems and robotics. Grounded in past research on the topic, it categorizes opportunities for choosing what to learn as coming from task decomposition or simplification for difficult problems and/or large environments; unsupervised pre‐training of representations and priors; multiagent learning; and learning from human interaction. The article is based closely on a keynote talk with the same title, delivered at the AAAI‐2026 conference in Singapore on January 22nd, 2026.

Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) has raised concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of synthetic media. Although AI disclosure labels are increasingly used as transparency mechanisms, the cognitive processes through which these cues influence trust formation remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to develop and test a cognitive pathway model explaining how AI disclosure labels, authenticity judgments, perceived risk, cognitive processing styles, and literacy factors shape trust toward AI-generated videos. Methods A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 617 participants randomly assigned to four conditions involving AI-generated instructional videos with different AI label and video quality combinations. Participants evaluated authenticity, systematic and heuristic processing, trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, sharing intention, AI literacy, and media literacy. Regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderation analyses were performed. Results AI disclosure labels significantly reduced perceived authenticity but did not directly affect trust, adoption, sharing intention, or perceived risk. Trust formation occurred through cognitive pathways: systematic processing increased trust, whereas heuristic processing reduced trust. Authenticity enhanced trust and lowered perceived risk, with perceived risk mediating the authenticity–trust relationship. Trust positively predicted adoption and sharing intentions, while AI and media literacy moderated selected relationships. Conclusion Trust in AI-generated videos was not directly determined by transparency labels alone. Instead, the observed associations among authenticity judgments, perceived risk, information processing, and trust were consistent with a multi-stage cognitive interpretation, although the cross-sectional post-exposure measurement of these constructs does not establish their temporal or causal sequence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Recent developments in AI are shifting the main source of risk from the flawed outputs of individual models to the unintended effects of agentic AI systems. Limited but growing evidence of misaligned behavior in swarms of AI agents suggests that such systems can pursue unassigned tasks and act beyond the reach of traditional corporate governance tools, which presuppose agents with interests, fiduciary duties and legal personality. This paper argues that the object of governance should be expanded from the model in isolation to the agentic AI system as a whole, and that oversight should be calibrated to the combined level of capability, autonomy, external access, permissions and scale. It proposes a framework of recursive governance, in which monitoring, evaluation, intervention and authorization form a continuous feedback loop rather than a fixed checklist. Four propositions follow: (P1) governance must become more stringent as capability and operational autonomy combine with external access and scale; (P2) autonomous deployment at a given capability level should not occur unless predefined criteria for evaluation, monitoring, containment and independent verification are met; (P3) some governance functions should be embedded in the technical architecture rather than being left solely to ex post human intervention; (P4) enforcement should rest on conditional and revocable access to the infrastructure that autonomous operation requires, with the kill switch as the last resort of a broader regime, and should be anchored as far as possible to institutions, rules and forms of self-regulation that already exist. To this end, the paper proposes a three-stage enforcement architecture: (i) a lean, independent multilateral agency, composed mainly of experts in advanced AI, certifies that the governance process for AI agents is actually followed; (ii) the certificate is fully incorporated into the ESG framework already operating in the European Union and linked to existing EU legislation on sustainability reporting, sustainable finance and ESG ratings; (iii) the IMF includes AI governance compliance in its periodic surveillance of member countries through the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP). Apart from the new agency, which to our knowledge does not yet exist, enforcement would thus rely on institutions that are already in place. The proposed policies are framed as responses to three market failures: information asymmetry, negative externalities and a collective action problem among competing developers (a safety race to the bottom). The last of these is to be addressed through common safety standards, not through any relaxation of antitrust rules.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In an AI-supported task, a student may explain a weak comparison once it has been identified, yet fail to notice a similar problem without a reminder. A decision about further help therefore needs evidence about what the student did without being prompted. We examine such decisions in English-medium university argumentation and evidence evaluation. The framework brings together English-language work on scaffolding, learner-generated reasoning, metacognitive calibration, and cognitive offloading. We distinguish help that supplies a reason from help that initiates a check. Readiness to work without the first does not establish readiness to work without the second. Coding examples and boundary cases make evidence about these functions interpretable, while six conditional propositions connect reconstruction and regulation to adaptation and transfer. A proposed experiment gives every group comparable diagnostic practice but varies whether teachers use its results to adjust assistance. This comparison isolates the value of using the evidence from learning through the diagnostic task itself. We relate the account to four GenAI approaches and illustrate it with a hypothetical sociology lesson. Help may be retained or restored when a new task requires it. The framework and coding rules need validation, particularly beyond the language and disciplinary settings considered here.

Precision medicine is reshaping medical imaging through artificial intelligence, quantitative biomarkers or hybrid modalities such as PET-CT. Yet these tools reach patients unevenly, and that unevenness is usually blamed on technical problems: interoperability, validation, trust. Drawing on management science and the sociology of professions, we propose a different explanation. What decides whether an innovation reaches patients equitably is not the technology, but the way it travels. We distinguish three ways of travelling. Diffusion is spontaneous spread through professional networks (letting it happen). Dissemination is spread deliberately directed towards a defined population (helping it happen). Implementation is the work of turning an adopted innovation into everyday routine (making it happen). Imaging innovations have travelled mainly by diffusion, which follows existing specialist density, funding rules and like-with-like professional networks; diffusion therefore reproduces the inequalities of access it inherits instead of correcting them. Three consequences follow. First, adoption hides three separate decisions taken by different people: acquiring the equipment, deciding what the examination actually contains, and deciding whether it is requested at all. Routine statistics count the first and the third; the second is never measured. Second, professional boundaries are held in place at once by regulation, by specialty jurisdiction and by everyday working relationships, so reforms acting on only one of them fail. Third, the medical report is where those boundaries meet: when it does not carry an integrated answer, the innovation stalls. A fourth point runs through all three: an innovation's value is not fixed before it travels; its construction is predicated on the expectations that precede it, and the practices through which it is utilised. Using a three-study programme on PET-CT in France as illustration, we argue that equitable and sustainable precision imaging is achieved not by buying equipment but by governing how innovations spread—including by actively retiring the low-value practices they were meant to replace, what management science calls exnovation.

documents.abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that viewers tend to evaluate AI-generated advertisements negatively. We argue that viewers can nevertheless enjoy creative advertisements produced by AI. However, the belief that creativity is an exclusively human attribute may prompt cognitive regulation when AI involvement is disclosed. Using a consumer neuroscience approach, we conducted a one-factor, three-level between-subjects experiment in which participants viewed advertisements with no disclosure, disclosure of human–AI collaboration, or disclosure of full AI creation. Creative advertisements elicited joy, captured by facial expression analysis, regardless of whether they were created by humans or AI. Greater joy was associated with less message counterarguing and more favourable advertisement attitudes, but only in the absence of AI disclosure. These findings suggest that AI disclosure does not diminish initial enjoyment. Instead, it may act as a persuasion knowledge cue that activates cognitive regulation, leading viewers to override their positive affective responses when subsequently evaluating the advertisement.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now employed in many visual design programs to create images rapidly, but these images may not meet the designer's expectations at first glance. This paper studies mismatch via text prompting, parameters and presets, reference-based input, and in-canvas manipulation. The fourteen academic sources in the review include thirteen peer-reviewed publications from 2024-2026 and Shneiderman's original work on direct manipulation. The workflow stage, participant group, interaction pattern, and the five dimensions of efficiency, perceived control, cognitive load, creative agency, and output predictability were used for evidence coding. Based on this evidence, the demand for refinement reduces the apparent advantage of rapid exploration. Effort saved in generation may be recovered by reducing prompt modifications, filtering output, or re-retrieving a suitable image. More local interactions help express and observe the decisions, but they do not eliminate the uncertainty in the generated results. Evidence for the parameters and presets is relatively scarce, so all four patterns cannot be evaluated equally. This framing clarifies how interface design, rather than model capability alone, affects professional agency and supports more informed tool selection in creative practice.

Open Educational Resources (OER) in higher education are shifting from models centred on the creation and storage of learning materials towards structures characterised by greater connectivity and institutionalisation. This study analyses this development across four dimensions: the emergence of repositories; infrastructure connectivity and interoperability; the institutionalisation of OER in association with Open Educational Practices (OEP); and the formation of adaptive OER ecosystems. Drawing on a review and mapping of the literature, policy analysis, and a comparison of selected prominent OER initiatives, the study conceptualises the development of OER as a five-level progression: repository, organised production, institutionalisation, ecosystem, and adaptive/AI-enabled ecosystem. The findings indicate that repositories constitute a necessary infrastructural condition, but are insufficient in themselves to ensure the effective use, reuse, and sustainability of OER. Interoperability, stakeholder capacities, pedagogical practices, policies, and governance mechanisms become increasingly important as OER expands. Accordingly, the study argues that an OER ecosystem should be understood as a structure comprising interconnected components that can adapt to technological change, particularly the development of generative AI.

The revised United States guidance on model risk management, issued in April 2026, applies its principles to traditional statistical and quantitative models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models, and places generative and agentic AI explicitly outside its scope. This survey follows the models used against fraud and financial crime across that line, from rules, scorecards, and statistical tests, through non-generative machine learning, to generative models and language-model agents, across six fraud types. Unlike prior surveys, we place all three generations in one decision-theoretic frame: we restate in one notation known results on cost-optimal and capacity-constrained alerting, undersampling calibration, and the identifiability of recall from alert feedback, express each generation's model, explanation, and validation quantity in that frame, and add two stylized models, one showing why mean aggregation dilutes the neighborhood signal of camouflaged fraudsters and one showing how verifier independence bounds the residual errors in a generated narrative. We find that statistical models and non-generative machine learning have mature validation practice anchored in supervisory guidance, that generative AI now appears both as a tool of fraudsters and as a component of defenses, and that in hybrid pipelines the generative component can write what an analyst or examiner reads although no dedicated supervisory framework covers it. We therefore formalize the evidence-traceability controls that can supply this missing validation as a division of verification labor, between the drafting agent, a deterministic field check, an independent verifier and the human examiner, governed by three parameters an institution can estimate; we then compare the generations quantity by quantity and close with a research agenda.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study comparatively examines the communication environments and practices of Generations Z, Alpha, and Beta within the framework of media ecology. Generations are treated not as biological age cohorts but as experiential and epistemic regimes shaped by the dominant communication medium. The study is not an empirical field investigation but offers a conceptual and typological comparison. It draws on established empirical literature for Generation Z, platform and interface studies along with child and media research for Generation Alpha, and critical discourse analysis of technology vision texts and the sociotechnical imaginaries approach for Generation Beta. The comparison proceeds along five parameters namely dominant medium, mode of interaction, content production model, epistemic authority, and socio-communicative role. The findings suggest a gradual shift in communication from network-based human-to-human interaction toward human-artificial intelligence interaction and a relocation of epistemic authority from peer groups and algorithmic feeds to personalized artificial intelligence agents. The study argues that this shift necessitates reconsidering the sender-receiver model alongside actor-network theory and the human-machine communication literature.

This chapter introduces the fundamental principles of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs) within the context of Sports Science and data-driven analytics. It demonstrates how unstructured textual and vocal data complement traditional numerical performance metrics by capturing contextual, psychological, and communicative aspects of sport environments. The chapter systematically presents core NLP techniques, including tokenization, lemmatization, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, topic modeling, and word embeddings, and explains their role in transforming language-based data into structured representations for performance analysis and decision-making. Building on these foundations, the chapter examines key neural network architectures used in NLP, particularly recurrent neural networks, Long Short-Term Memory models, and Transformer-based systems. Special emphasis is placed on the attention mechanism and its role in enabling scalable and context-aware language modelling. The chapter further analyzes the capabilities and limitations of Large Language Models, including their generative potential, adaptability through fine-tuning and prompt-based interaction, and challenges such as hallucinations, bias, and interpretability. Through multimodal integration and applied case studies, the chapter highlights how NLP and LLMs contribute to sports analytics, athlete monitoring, talent identification, and real-time decision-making.

Lunar exploration has shifted from single flights to a planned buildup of permanent infrastructure. NASA flew four astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II in April 2026, and within eight weeks announced the first three robotic Moon Base missions along with close to a billion dollars in contracts for surface rovers, cargo landers and hopping drones. A parallel programme led by China and Russia, the International Lunar Research Station, is working towards a basic configuration by 2035 with a nuclear power unit delivered between 2033 and 2035. This paper examines the machines that will carry out most of the work in both programmes. It sets out the supervised autonomy model that governs how humans and robots divide decisions under communication delay, identifies the specific artificial intelligence techniques that lunar robots depend on, and proposes an interaction protocol for surface operations. The paper then turns to security. Nearly every capability needed for lunar construction, survey and resource extraction has an obvious military application, and the argument advanced here is that any confrontation on the Moon would be short, machine-led and fought over access to a small number of usable sites rather than over territory in the terrestrial sense. Gaps in the Outer Space Treaty and in the Artemis Accords are assessed against that prospect.

Introduction: Gamification incorporates game design elements into educational activities and offers opportunities to strengthen student participation. However, its effects depend on planning, curricular objectives and implementation conditions. The aim was to analyse its relationship with student motivation and identify opportunities and challenges relevant to Ecuadorian upper secondary education. Methodology: A narrative review of twenty publications on motivational foundations, gamification and learning was developed, incorporating international contributions and a review situated in Ecuador. The synthesis addressed four dimensions: foundations, motivation, pedagogical opportunities and implementation challenges. Published findings were distinguished from teaching guidance derived from their interpretation. Results: The reviewed meta-analyses report favourable, although variable, effects on cognitive, motivational and behavioural outcomes. Evidence specifically concerning intrinsic motivation indicates a small effect, alongside improvements in autonomy and relatedness and a smaller effect on perceived competence. Feedback, progressive challenges and collaboration offer pedagogical possibilities, whereas controlling rewards, exclusionary competition, access barriers and assessment restricted to points require attention. Conclusions: Gamification can enrich teaching when game elements are linked to verifiable learning and inclusive participation opportunities. Its application to Ecuadorian upper secondary education requires contextual adaptation and assessment of understanding and sustained motivation. The narrative approach and diversity of sources limit generalisation and do not permit attribution of effects to specific institutions or causal conclusions about the Ecuadorian school context.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Heritage museums balance a dual mission: preserving culture and providing educational experiences. As institutions adopt AI-generated audio guides, narrator acoustic features—such as gender and age—significantly impact visitor experiences. This study examines how AI narrator gender and age influence Korean-English bilingual youths’ (ages 15–24) perceptions across two domains: the cultural function (belonging and empathy) and the educational function (comprehensibility and professionalism). Utilizing a between-subjects design, 71 participants were randomly assigned to one of four AI voice conditions (young/old, female/male) to evaluate audio guides for two heritage sites (Korea’s Geunjeongjeon and France’s Hall of Mirrors). A two-way ANOVA revealed older voices yielded significantly higher scores across both functions. For the educational function, male voices independently scored higher than females. For the cultural function, a significant interaction emerged, with older male voices scoring highest. These findings demonstrate that AI voices are not merely neutral information-delivery tools, but active social cues that shape cultural resonance and credibility. Older voices were associated with higher perceived educational and cultural function ratings, while older male voices received the highest cultural-function rating. Consequently, the study suggests that museums must move beyond default voice settings and strategically align AI personas with specific communicative goals.

This review examined how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can widen educational opportunity while also reproducing social inequality. An integrative review synthesized 24 sources: 17 Indonesian publications (2022–2026), identified through national journal portals and Google Scholar, and seven international policy documents and scholarly works (2016–2023) selected as conceptual anchors. Thematic analysis produced four themes: unequal access, unequal digital and AI literacy, unequal capacity to benefit from AI-supported learning, and governance risks involving privacy, bias, academic integrity, and human agency. The reported benefits of generative AI, such as tutoring, writing support, and translation, appear to depend on connectivity, devices, language resources, teacher competence, and students' ability to evaluate machine output. The Indonesian evidence is mostly cross-sectional, self-reported, or based on small single-institution samples, with little evidence on learning outcomes. One national household analysis of school participation (not AI use) found no significant difference between 3T (disadvantaged, frontier, and outermost) and matched non-3T households, suggesting that regional labels may be an imperfect proxy for household conditions. The review proposes a cumulative model of AI inequality that extends van Dijk's sequence of digital inequality with a governance stage and a feedback loop. The model is a conceptual proposition, not a tested result, and recommendations are ordered by the strength of supporting evidence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping content production in the cultural and creative industries by shifting cultural material organization, script writing, exhibition interpretation, and cultural tourism communication from linear manual workflows to human-AI collaborative workflows. Focusing on productivity improvement and the boundary of creative labor substitution, this research constructs a three-group comparison framework involving human-only creation, AI-assisted creation, and fully AI-generated creation. Based on public cultural heritage data, cultural policy texts, and cultural tourism communication samples from 2018 to 2024, LLMs, RAG, Sentence-BERT semantic retrieval, expert scoring, and mixed-effects ANOVA are combined to measure generation quality, policy suitability, and substitution intensity across different cultural tasks. The results show that the average completion time of the AI-assisted group decreases from 44.2 min to 25.7 min, while the overall quality score increases from 82.6 to 84.1, indicating that human-AI collaboration can improve production efficiency while maintaining content quality. Although the fully AI-generated group achieves the lowest time cost, its policy suitability and cultural accuracy decline noticeably. Task complexity further affects substitution intensity. Cultural tourism copy and short-video scripts are more substitutable, while exhibition interpretation and policy explanation still rely on human judgment. These findings provide quantitative evidence for AI adoption, creative labor restructuring, and cultural policy governance.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.

documents.abstract: Against the backdrop of educational evaluation reform, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) has been increasingly applied to performance assessment, yet its actual effects and challenges remain underexplored. This study surveyed 50 undergraduate students to examine their perceptions of GAI-based performance assessment across five dimensions: evaluation efficiency and feedback timeliness, accuracy and fairness, appropriateness of scoring criteria and weight distribution, stability and trust, and deep learning and innovation. Results show that over 70% of respondents recognized GAI's advantages in scoring speed and feedback timeliness, and most regarded its scoring criteria as clear and consistent. However, nearly 75% believed GAI failed to identify innovative highlights, over 70% perceived a tendency to emphasize form over content, and 44% reported that such preferences constrained their creative expression. Respondents also raised concerns about incorrect information, technical instability, and the lack of emotional interaction compared with human evaluation. These findings suggest that GAI should act as an auxiliary tool rather than a full replacement for teacher evaluation. To address current limitations, it is necessary to improve GAI's deep evaluation and fact-checking capabilities, establish human-machine collaborative review mechanisms, and cultivate students' critical thinking. This study provides implications for integrating GAI into university performance assessment.

Nail art has evolved from a decorative beauty practice into a personalized cosmetic service that reflects individual image, style, and self-expression. Nevertheless, nail color selection remains largely dependent on personal preference, fashion trends, social-media images, and practitioner experience rather than standardized color-harmony criteria. This integrative review examines how objective skin color science, nail art design characteristics, personal color concepts, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be combined to establish a methodological basis for personalized nail color selection. The literature on human skin color measurement, CIELAB colorimetry, color-difference analysis, personal color and nail color matching, virtual beauty technologies, and skin-tone bias in AI-generated imagery was synthesized. The evidence supports representing hand skin color as a multidimensional profile based on L*, a*, b*, chroma, and hue angle rather than relying solely on warm/cool or seasonal categories. Nail art should likewise be described using colorimetric, optical, reflective, decorative, and compositional features. Generative AI offers a scalable means of creating standardized virtual hand–nail stimuli, but current evidence demonstrates substantial skin-tone imbalance and potential color inaccuracy in generated images. We therefore propose a six-stage framework: hand skin-color profiling, nail-art feature classification, generative AI-based virtual image generation, colorimetric accuracy and bias validation, skin–nail harmony modeling, and personalized guideline development. This framework should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than as a validated recommendation system. External validation using objectively measured human hand skin color and perceptual evaluation is required before clinical, commercial, or professional implementation.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market, yet it remains unclear whether students’ appraisal of AI-driven employment threat translates into employment anxiety in similar ways across cultural groups. This study administered an online questionnaire to 1,595 domestic students (1,095) and international students (500) enrolled at Central South University. Perceived AI replacement threat, AI optimism, and employment anxiety were assessed with 13 five-point Likert items. Information channels, coping behaviors, desired institutional support, and perceived coping relief were assessed as supplementary measures. Confirmatory factor analyses supported an acceptable three-factor structure in both groups. The distinction between threat and anxiety remained qualified due to their substantial association. Metric invariance was established, and partial scalar invariance was obtained after the intercept of Q21 was freed. Perceived AI replacement threat and employment anxiety remained empirically distinguishable, although their latent correlation was stronger among international students than among domestic students. In the structural model, threat was strongly associated with anxiety ( β = 0.764) and weakly associated with optimism ( β = 0.133). After threat was included, optimism showed a small negative conditional association with anxiety ( β = −0.152). The indirect association through optimism was negative but limited in magnitude, and equivalent cross-sectional specifications fit the data equally well. This pattern is best interpreted as an exploratory statistical finding compatible with suppression, rather than confirmed evidence of a directional psychological mechanism. Supplementary coping analyses were descriptive and exploratory. These findings provide qualified empirical support for a three-factor framework of students’ responses to AI-related employment uncertainty, and highlight differences in threat-anxiety coupling across student populations. The results carry implications for targeted student support services addressing AI-related career concerns.

As generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into education and teaching, the question of how to leverage teachers' professional judgment and achieve effective human-machine collaboration has become a significant issue. Based on the theories of AI-TPACK and SAMR, this study focuses on the human-machine co-creation mechanism in the design of high school English teaching activities supported by generative AI. The research employs semi-structured interviews and design-based research methods. By interviewing three high school English teachers, their AI-TPACK performance and practical dilemmas are analyzed. Subsequently, a human-machine co-creation teaching operation model is constructed, and two rounds of practice are carried out in a high school English poetry appreciation course. The research findings indicate that teachers have developed a certain awareness of AI integration, yet they still encounter problems such as poor adaptation to students' learning situations, insufficient output evaluation, and inadequate collaboration mechanisms. The practice shows that continuous negotiation, evaluation, and reconstruction under teachers' guidance are the keys to achieving effective human-machine co-creation.

documents.abstract: Abstract Prior studies exploring teachers’ perceptions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini have signaled tensions between instructors’ perceptions of GenAI’s usefulness and their beliefs regarding its ethicality. The current study furthers this line of inquiry, examining issues of ethics and utility by focusing specifically on teachers of languages other than English. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, this study employed a survey to understand language instructors’ ( N = 101) perceptions of the ethicality of GenAI tool use in higher education, along with their perceptions of the usefulness of GenAI for supporting second language (L2) learning. Semi-structured interviews were then conducted with six teachers to further understand participants’ survey responses, with some teachers sharing additional artifacts (e.g., course policies regarding GenAI). The findings suggest that most teachers (92.1%) believe GenAI tools are ethical if used for specific purposes. There also appears to be a connection between teachers’ ethical beliefs and their perceptions of GenAI’s utility, in terms of whether GenAI is used by students as a scaffold/support mechanism versus being used to produce content. The implications of this study provide a roadmap for developing discipline-specific guidelines that preserve L2 learning integrity while leveraging GenAI’s utility.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly explored across health care for clinical decision-making and education. Within digital health, workforce readiness and digital capability are recognized as critical to successful technology implementation. Midwifery faces persistent workforce challenges including limited protected learning time, restricted leadership development opportunities, and unclear career pathways, yet it is unclear whether generative AI has been examined as a tool to support midwifery workforce development. A scoping review was conducted following the framework of Arksey and O’Malley with PRISMA-ScR reporting. EBSCOhost (CINAHL, MEDLINE, ERIC), Google Scholar, and Elicit were searched for English-language studies published between 2015 and 2026 examining AI in midwifery in relation to at least one of the following: post-registration education, workforce, professional development, leadership, and career progression. Findings were synthesized using framework analysis. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Research focused predominantly on clinical decision-making, predictive models, and undergraduate education. No studies examined generative AI tools to support practicing midwives’ professional development, leadership, or career progression. Attitudes towards AI varied with digital literacy, generational cohort, and ethical concerns. Generative AI in midwifery workforce development is unexamined in the empirical literature. Further research is required to understand acceptability, risks, and value within an ethically governed implementation framework.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is reshaping health sciences education. For nursing students, educational interaction (EI), self-regulated learning (SRL), and GAI interaction are all particularly important. However, these relationships and their processes remain underexplored. Methods A total of 1020 nursing students were recruited from one medical university in Hunan Province in China. The Demographics Questionnaire, the Chinese version of Student-GAI interaction scale, the Educational Interaction Scale, and the Self-regulated Learning Questionnaire were administered. SPSS 22.0 and AMOS 24.0 software were used to analyze the data. Results The mean scores of student-GAI interaction (SGI) and EI were 14.80 ± 2.27 and 70.90 ± 8.15, respectively. Significant positive relationships were found among all three variables (all P < 0.01). Both SGI (β = 0.256) and SRL (β = 0.520) positively were associated with EI (both P < 0.001). Furthermore, SGI showed a significant direct association with EI, with a direct effect value of 0.92 ( P < 0.001). SRL statistically mediated the association between SGI and EI, with a significant indirect effect value of 0.44. The mediating effect represented 32.35% of the total effect ( P < 0.001). Dimension-specific analyses revealed that the mediating effect was strongest for student-teacher interaction (45.41%) and student-content interaction (41.54%). Conclusions SGI is positively associated with EI among nursing students, both directly and indirectly through SRL. Educational strategies that encourage effective GAI use and strengthen SRL may be associated with enhanced EI in nursing education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the governance of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science academia, emphasizing the intersection of regulatory frameworks, educational practice, and academic integrity. It argues that AI governance in sport must extend beyond general data protection and transparency concerns to address domain-specific risks related to athlete welfare, informed consent, and high-stakes decision-making. The chapter presents a comparative analysis of global regulatory models, including the European Union’s risk-based approach, the United States’ soft-law framework, and diverse Asian and South American strategies, highlighting their implications for academic research and data governance in sport contexts. Further, the chapter explores the integration of AI governance into academic publishing and higher education, outlining converging principles such as human accountability, mandatory disclosure of AI use, and the prohibition of AI authorship. It introduces a harmonic model of AI integration based on active use, critical supervision, and epistemic accountability, positioning AI as a supportive but inherently fallible tool. The chapter also conceptualizes AI literacy as a core competence in sports science education and proposes a structured curriculum governance framework that integrates ethical reasoning, uncertainty interpretation, and responsible AI use. Collectively, the chapter provides a comprehensive foundation for aligning technological innovation with regulatory compliance, educational transformation, and the preservation of scientific integrity in Sports Science.

documents.abstract: The project defines a test environment inspired by the time-loop mechanism featured in the film Groundhog Day. An agent attempts to complete a task; if it makes an error classified as fatal (or exhausts its step budget), the environment is restored to a previously saved checkpoint, while the agent retains a complete, structured memory of all previous loops: the loop counter, cumulative time, summaries of failed attempts, and its own hypotheses. Unlike a conventional episode reset in reinforcement learning (RL), failure information is not lost—it becomes a persistent part of the agent's observations. Additionally, after a reset, the environment may slightly mutate the task conditions, but only when necessary to force the agent to change its strategy (the minimal-intervention principle). These mutations are observable to the agent but are never explicitly signaled. Project objectives: - C1. Build a measurable benchmark for agents' ability to perform within-episode meta-learning (in-context adaptation across resets): the agent should learn from failures without updating its weights. - C2. Investigate whether explicit loop memory reduces time to success compared with an agent without memory (control-group experiments). - C3. Investigate whether minimal changes to task conditions disrupt strategy lock-in, i.e., a situation in which an agent repeatedly attempts variations of the same flawed strategy despite having complete memory of its failures. - C4. Provide a reproducible, deterministic (seeded) harness for experiments with RL agents and LLM-based agents, using a single, unified evaluation protocol. - C5. Identify and measure undesirable emergent behaviors: reward hacking through deliberately triggering resets, learned helplessness, and overfitting to the mutation pattern. Out of scope: gradient-based weight training across loops (the project evaluates in-context adaptation through memory, not through-gradient meta-learning); physical real-time simulation. Artifacts: github.com/casual-art/Groudhog-Day (harness, docs); archive DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23483377.

Aim: This study compared the guideline adherence, clinical safety, risk stratification, source accuracy, and practical applicability of three commercial large language models in perioperative GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) and dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor agonist (GLP-1/GIP RA) management scenarios.Methods: In this non-interventional scenario-based comparative study, 20 English-language perioperative clinical scenarios were submitted once to ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and Gemini Advanced/Google AI Pro. documents.abstract: This article presents the results of a theoretical-conceptual study based on a critical analysis of the relevant philosophical literature. The central concepts were traced across the philosophical literature and, on the basis of that analysis, ethical prolepsis is proposed as an attitude of the operative subject toward the foreseeable consequences of their actions, an attitude grounded in accumulated experience and constitutively practical in its orientation, that is, always referred to effective courses of action rather than to formal principles detached from praxis. It is found that, although the anticipatory disposition can be identified at various points in the Western philosophical tradition, it has in no case received a formulation that situates it as an ethical attitude of primary standing, and it is precisely that omission which this work aims to help redress. As part of the proposal, the manifestations of the proleptic attitude are established at the individual and social levels, and its specific relevance to the phenomenon of artificial intelligence (AI) is argued, with attention to the problem of anthropomorphization, whose epistemic and moral consequences are briefly examined in relation to epistemic agency, moral agency, responsibility gaps, and biocomputation.
